title.zh: 第一部分 - 预订度假公寓

sections.passage:
A man calls a holiday rental company to book an apartment for a family holiday. The booking agent, Sophie, assists him with the reservation.

The man explains that he wants to book an apartment for a week in August for his family of four, including himself, his wife, and their two teenage children. They are looking for a property in the coastal town of Santa Marina. Sophie checks the available properties and finds three options that match their requirements.

The first option is Apartment 4B in the Marina Complex, which is a two-bedroom apartment on the third floor with a balcony overlooking the sea. It has a fully equipped kitchen, air conditioning, and Wi-Fi. The weekly rate in August is 850 euros. However, it only has one bathroom, which Sophie notes might be inconvenient for a family of four.

The second option is Apartment 7A in the same complex, which is a three-bedroom apartment on the fifth floor. It has two bathrooms, a large living area, a kitchen with a dishwasher, and a rooftop terrace with panoramic views. The weekly rate is 1,100 euros, which includes cleaning service twice a week. The man thinks this sounds ideal but wants to confirm the cost.

The third option is a ground-floor apartment in the Villa Rosa building, located 200 meters from the beach. It has three bedrooms, two bathrooms, a private garden, and a shared swimming pool. The weekly rate is 950 euros, but there is an additional charge of 60 euros for the final cleaning.

The man decides to book Apartment 7A. Sophie asks for his details to complete the booking. His name is David Thompson, and his email is d.thompson@email.com. His phone number is 07903 456712. Sophie confirms that a 30 percent deposit of 330 euros is required now, with the balance of 770 euros due four weeks before arrival. The company accepts payment by credit card or bank transfer. David chooses to pay by credit card. Sophie sends a confirmation email with all the booking details and arrival instructions.

title.en: Section 2 - Introduction to a City Walking Tour
title.zh: 第二部分 - 城市步行游览介绍

sections.passage:
Good morning and welcome to the Heritage City Walking Tour. My name is Robert, and I'll be your guide this morning. Before we set off, I'd like to give you an overview of what we'll be seeing and some important practical information.

Our tour covers approximately 3 kilometers and will take about two and a half hours, including two comfort stops. We'll be walking at a leisurely pace, so don't worry about keeping up. The route is mostly flat, but there is one steep hill near the end, so wear comfortable shoes. The tour operates rain or shine, and we have complimentary umbrellas available if needed.

Our first stop will be the Old Town Hall, which was built in 1785 and is considered one of the finest examples of Georgian architecture in the country. It served as the seat of local government until 1962 and is now a museum of local history. We'll spend about fifteen minutes here, during which you can explore the council chamber and the exhibition of historical photographs.

From there, we'll walk through the Merchant's Quarter, a collection of narrow medieval streets that once housed the shops and workshops of the city's wealthiest traders. The oldest building in this area dates back to 1320. Several of these buildings have been converted into independent shops, galleries, and cafes, and I'd recommend coming back to explore them at your leisure after the tour.

We'll then cross the Old Bridge, which was originally built in 1480 and has been widened twice, in 1820 and 1965. The bridge offers excellent views of the cathedral and the river. After the bridge, we'll visit the cathedral, which was constructed between 1180 and 1420. The cathedral's famous stained glass windows, dating from the 13th century, are considered among the finest in Europe.

Our final stop will be the Castle Gardens, a beautifully landscaped park that surrounds the ruins of the medieval castle. The castle was built in 1068 by William the Conqueror and was largely destroyed during the English Civil War in 1648. The gardens were redesigned in the Victorian era and feature a bandstand, a lake, and a collection of rare trees. We'll finish the tour at the Castle Gardens cafe, where you can enjoy refreshments.

Tickets for the tour cost 12 pounds for adults, 8 pounds for seniors and students, and children under 12 go free. Family tickets for two adults and up to three children are available at 28 pounds. All tickets include admission to the Old Town Hall museum. You can book tickets at our website or at the tourist information center on Market Square.

title.en: Section 3 - Two Students Planning a Geology Field Trip
title.zh: 第三部分 - 两名学生规划地质实地考察

sections.passage:
Emma and Jack are second-year geology students planning a field trip to Dorset for their coursework assignment. They meet in the library to discuss their plans.

Emma has been researching the Dorset coastline, which is famous for its geological significance. The Jurassic Coast, stretching 154 kilometers from Exmouth in Devon to Old Harry Rocks in Dorset, was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001. It is one of the most important geological sites in the world, with rocks spanning 185 million years of Earth's history, from the Triassic through the Jurassic to the Cretaceous periods.

They plan to focus their field trip on three specific sites along the coast. The first site is Lulworth Cove, a spectacular horseshoe-shaped bay formed by the erosion of softer rocks behind a harder limestone band. Here they will examine the exposed rock layers and collect samples of limestone, chalk, and clay. They need to bring geological hammers, sample bags, and field notebooks. Emma suggests they also bring a hand lens for examining mineral crystals and a dilute hydrochloric acid bottle for testing carbonate rocks.

The second site is Durdle Door, a natural limestone arch located about one kilometer west of Lulworth Cove. This site is particularly valuable for studying the processes of coastal erosion and the formation of arches, stacks, and stumps. Jack has found a research paper by Dr. Collins at Bournemouth University that provides detailed measurements of the arch's dimensions and the rate of erosion over the past 50 years, which will be useful for their analysis.

The third site is the fossil-rich beach at Lyme Regis, famous as the location where Mary Anning discovered the first complete Ichthyosaurus skeleton in 1811. They hope to find ammonite and belemnite fossils, which are abundant in the Jurassic limestone cliffs. Emma mentions that the best time to search for fossils is after winter storms, which erode the cliff face and expose new specimens. Since they are visiting in spring, they may need to be patient and search carefully among the shingle.

Regarding logistics, they plan to travel by train to Wareham, then take a local bus to Lulworth. The total travel time from the university is approximately three hours. They will need to arrange accommodation for two nights, and Jack has found a youth hostel in Wareham that charges 22 pounds per person per night. They need to submit their field trip proposal to Dr. Harrison by Friday and can begin their fieldwork from the following Monday.

title.en: Section 4 - Lecture on the History of Glass Manufacturing
title.zh: 第四部分 - 关于玻璃制造历史的讲座

sections.passage:
Good afternoon, everyone. Today's lecture continues our series on materials science by examining the remarkable history of glass, one of the most versatile and widely used materials in the modern world. Glass is all around us, from the windows in our homes to the screens on our smartphones, yet few people appreciate the extraordinary technical achievements that have made modern glass products possible.

Glass-making is an ancient craft, with the earliest known glass objects dating back to around 3500 BC in Mesopotamia and Egypt. These early glass items were small decorative beads and vessels, produced by wrapping molten glass around a core of sand. The technique of glass blowing, which revolutionized the industry by making it possible to produce hollow vessels quickly and cheaply, was invented by craftsmen in the Syro-Palestinian region around 50 BC. This innovation made glass containers accessible to ordinary households for the first time, replacing the ceramic pots and metal vessels that had previously been used for storing liquids.

For the next 2,000 years, glass-making techniques improved gradually but remained essentially a manual craft. The Industrial Revolution brought the first major mechanization of glass production. In 1903, Michael Owens of the Owens Bottle Machine Company in Toledo, Ohio, patented an automatic bottle-making machine that could produce 2,500 bottles per hour, compared to the 150 per hour achievable by a skilled human glassblower. This machine transformed the bottle industry and led to dramatic reductions in the cost of bottled goods.

The development of flat glass production has been equally revolutionary. As we discussed in last week's lecture, the float glass process, developed by Sir Alastair Pilkington in 1959, made it possible to produce large sheets of perfectly flat glass at a fraction of the cost of earlier methods. Today, the global glass industry produces approximately 130 million tonnes of glass per year, with flat glass accounting for about 40 percent of total production.

One of the most exciting areas of modern glass research is the development of ultra-thin flexible glass. Corning Incorporated, the American specialty glass manufacturer, has developed a product called Willow Glass that is just 0.1 millimeters thick and can be rolled up like a sheet of paper. This material has enormous potential for use in flexible displays, solar panels, and wearable technology. Samsung and LG have already demonstrated prototype smartphones with flexible glass screens that can be folded in half without breaking.

Another frontier is self-healing glass, which researchers at the University of Tokyo have demonstrated in the laboratory. This material, made from a low-weight polymer called polyether-thiourea, can repair itself at room temperature when cracked, simply by pressing the broken edges together for about 30 seconds. While still in the early stages of development, self-healing glass could eventually be used in smartphone screens, car windscreens, and building windows, potentially saving billions of pounds in replacement costs and reducing glass waste.

The glass industry also faces significant environmental challenges. Glass production is highly energy-intensive, requiring temperatures of over 1,500 degrees Celsius to melt the raw materials. The industry accounts for approximately 1 percent of global industrial carbon emissions. However, glass is one of the most recyclable materials available, and recycling it uses only about 25 percent of the energy needed to produce new glass from raw materials. In some European countries, glass recycling rates exceed 90 percent, demonstrating the potential for significant environmental improvements through better waste management.

sections.passage:
Millions of wells are found across the Indian subcontinent, but only a small proportion are stepwells, structures that combine a well with a series of steps leading down to the water level. Stepwells are a distinctive feature of the arid and semi-arid regions of western India, particularly the states of Gujarat and Rajasthan, where water scarcity has been a recurring challenge for thousands of years.

The earliest known stepwells date from around 600 AD, though the tradition may be considerably older. The construction of stepwells reached its peak between the 11th and 16th centuries, when hundreds of elaborate structures were built by wealthy patrons, including kings, merchants, and religious leaders. Stepwells served multiple purposes: they were practical water sources, particularly during the dry season when surface water was scarce; they were social gathering places where women in particular could meet and socialize away from the restrictions of everyday life; and they were religious and architectural monuments that demonstrated the wealth and piety of their builders.

The construction of a stepwell was a major engineering undertaking. Workers had to dig deep into the earth, sometimes to depths of over 100 feet, to reach the water table. The walls of the stepwell were lined with precisely cut stone blocks, fitted together without mortar, and the steps were carefully graded to allow easy access to the water at any level. Many stepwells included elaborate architectural features such as carved pillars, ornate archways, and sculptured niches depicting gods, animals, and scenes from daily life. The most impressive stepwells, such as the Rani ki Vav in Patan, Gujarat, which is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site, are essentially inverted temples descending into the earth.

The decline of stepwells began during the British colonial period. The British regarded traditional water management systems as primitive and introduced modern piped water systems and concrete dams as replacements. Many stepwells fell into disrepair as a result, and some were deliberately filled in to prevent the spread of disease, as stagnant water in abandoned wells was thought to harbor mosquitoes and other disease carriers. By the mid-20th century, most stepwells had ceased to function as water sources and were being used, if at all, as garbage dumps or latrines.

In recent years, there has been a growing movement to restore and preserve India's stepwells. Conservation groups, academic researchers, and local communities have joined forces to document and restore these remarkable structures. The organization Stepwell.in has catalogued over 2,000 stepwells across India and advocates for their recognition as significant cultural heritage sites. Some restored stepwells have been brought back into use as water sources, providing a sustainable alternative to deep bore wells, which have been depleting groundwater reserves across the region.

The renewed interest in stepwells is part of a broader recognition that traditional water management systems in India and other developing countries often represent sophisticated and sustainable approaches to water scarcity that modern engineering has overlooked. By studying and reviving these ancient techniques, researchers hope to develop new strategies for managing water resources in an era of increasing climate uncertainty and growing water demand.

sections.passage:
Sustainable transport policies have been a growing concern for European governments since the early 1990s. The European Union has been particularly active in developing transport policies that aim to balance economic growth with environmental protection and social equity. The period from 1990 to 2010 saw significant changes in European transport systems, driven by EU policy, technological innovation, and changing consumer behavior.

Road transport has consistently been the dominant mode of freight and passenger transport in Europe. In 2010, road vehicles accounted for approximately 73 percent of all inland freight transport in the EU and about 80 percent of passenger travel. Despite repeated policy commitments to shift freight from road to rail and waterway, the share of road transport has remained stubbornly high. This is partly because road transport offers greater flexibility and door-to-door convenience than other modes, and partly because the infrastructure costs of road transport are not fully reflected in the prices that users pay.

Rail transport, by contrast, has seen its share of both freight and passenger transport decline over the period. In 1990, rail accounted for approximately 15 percent of inland freight transport; by 2010, this had fallen to about 10 percent. For passenger transport, rail's share remained relatively stable at around 6 to 8 percent. However, high-speed rail services have grown significantly, with the total network expanding from about 1,200 kilometers in 1990 to over 7,000 kilometers by 2010. France's TGV, Spain's AVE, and Germany's ICE services have attracted millions of passengers from both airlines and conventional rail services on routes where high-speed trains offer competitive journey times.

Air transport experienced the most dramatic growth during this period. Passenger numbers at EU airports increased from approximately 400 million in 1990 to over 800 million in 2010, driven partly by the liberalization of the European aviation market and the rise of low-cost carriers such as Ryanair and easyJet. The number of routes served by low-cost carriers increased from fewer than 50 in 1990 to over 2,000 by 2010. However, this growth has come at a significant environmental cost, as aviation is one of the most carbon-intensive forms of transport. A single return flight from London to New York generates approximately 1.2 tonnes of carbon dioxide per passenger, which is roughly equivalent to the annual emissions from driving a car in Europe.

Cycling and walking, the most sustainable forms of transport, have received increasing policy attention over the period. Several European cities have invested heavily in cycling infrastructure, with Copenhagen and Amsterdam leading the way. However, the overall share of cycling and walking in total urban trips has declined in most EU countries, from approximately 40 percent in 1990 to about 30 percent in 2010, as car ownership has increased and urban sprawl has made distances between destinations longer.

The European Commission has set ambitious targets for reducing transport emissions. The 2011 Transport White Paper aims to reduce transport greenhouse gas emissions by 60 percent by 2050 compared to 1990 levels. Achieving this target will require a combination of technological solutions, including more efficient vehicles and alternative fuels, behavioral changes such as reduced car dependency and increased use of public transport, and policy measures such as carbon pricing and congestion charging.

sections.passage:
Innovation is widely recognized as a key driver of economic growth and competitive advantage. Yet despite its importance, innovation remains poorly understood. Why do some individuals and organizations consistently produce groundbreaking ideas while others, despite having access to similar resources and talent, fail to innovate? Research in cognitive psychology and organizational behavior suggests that the answer lies not in intelligence or technical expertise, but in the way people think and in the organizational cultures that either encourage or suppress creative thinking.

One of the most important cognitive traits associated with innovation is what psychologists call 'associative thinking,' the ability to connect ideas from different domains that are not obviously related. The late Steve Jobs famously described this ability when he said, 'Creativity is just connecting things.' Research by Professor Dean Keith Simonton at the University of California has shown that the most creative individuals tend to have broad interests and diverse knowledge bases, rather than deep expertise in a single field. They read widely, travel extensively, and expose themselves to a variety of cultures and perspectives.

Another key factor is tolerance of ambiguity and uncertainty. Innovative thinkers are comfortable with not having all the answers and are willing to pursue ideas whose outcomes are uncertain. Psychologist Abraham Maslow observed that creative individuals have a unusual capacity to tolerate disorder, confusion, and apparent chaos. They can hold contradictory ideas in their minds simultaneously and are not troubled by the tension this creates. This is in contrast to more conventional thinkers, who tend to resolve ambiguity quickly by choosing the most familiar or comfortable option.

The role of failure in innovation has been extensively studied. Research consistently shows that highly innovative individuals and organizations experience high rates of failure, but they treat failure as a learning opportunity rather than a disaster. Thomas Edison, who held over 1,000 patents, reportedly said, 'I have not failed. I've just found 10,000 ways that won't work.' Companies like Google and 3M famously encourage employees to spend a portion of their time on projects that may fail, recognizing that breakthrough innovations often emerge from unexpected experiments.

Organizational culture plays a crucial role in fostering or inhibiting innovation. Research by Harvard Business School professor Teresa Amabile has identified several key features of innovative organizations. These include giving employees autonomy to pursue their own ideas, providing adequate resources and time for experimentation, creating a psychologically safe environment where people can propose unconventional ideas without fear of ridicule or punishment, and ensuring that ideas are evaluated on their merits rather than on the status of the person who proposed them. Organizations that are highly hierarchical, risk-averse, or focused exclusively on short-term results tend to be less innovative.

The physical environment can also influence creative thinking. A study by the University of Minnesota found that people in rooms with higher ceilings performed better on creative tasks than those in rooms with lower ceilings, suggesting that physical space affects mental space. Similarly, research has shown that exposure to nature, even through a window view or photographs, can enhance creative performance. Companies like Apple, Google, and Pixar have invested heavily in designing office spaces that encourage spontaneous interaction and creative collaboration, with features such as open-plan layouts, communal areas, and recreational facilities.

Understanding the psychology of innovation has practical implications for education, business, and public policy. Educational systems that emphasize rote memorization and standardized testing may inadvertently suppress the creative thinking skills that are essential for innovation. Businesses that want to become more innovative need to think carefully about how their organizational structures, cultures, and physical environments affect the way their employees think and work. And governments seeking to promote innovation should consider investing not just in science and technology, but also in arts education, cross-cultural exchange, and other activities that broaden people's perspectives and develop their capacity for associative thinking.
